chapter_theme: The second part of the heading பகைத்திறம் தெரிதல் (verses 298-310) treats the craft of enmity: an open enemy is better than a false intimate, anger should stop when the enemy is dead, the petty are not worth fighting, allies in number outweigh one's own prowess, and above all an enemy is beaten by turning others against him, a rear threat, an outside power, the division within his own camp, and finally by the four means of words, gifts, division and measured force.

298.reading: The verse asks whether those who take up open enmity and keep apart are worse than those who, caring nothing for a man, attach themselves to him as his own and bring him blame in this life and sin for the next, and answers that blindness is better than dim sight.
298.nuance: செம்மைப் பகை, 'straight enmity', is set against the false kinsman: the proverb ranks a known lack (blindness) above a sight that seems to see and misleads (மைம்மை, a clouded eye). The harm of the false friend is counted in two worlds, blame here and sin hereafter, which the open enemy cannot cause.

pazhamozhi.literal: blindness is better than clouded sight

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the false intimate set against the open enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an open enemy is less harmful than one who poses as one's own

299.reading: To go on raging beyond measure, unsettled, even after one has fought and killed those who would not agree, is like flooding the stubble with water after the crop has been reaped.
299.nuance: The proverb's point is waste: water given to a reaped field feeds nothing. The verse does not blame the killing; it blames the anger that outlives its object. The address வெற்ப!, 'man of the hills', is the poet's frame, not the audience.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anger that continues after the enemy is destroyed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: rage after the enemy is dead is labour without fruit

300.reading: Even if the great take on the enmity of men of hard strength, to take on the enmity of men of low standing brings them nothing, for even a light shower can bring a flood.
300.nuance: The proverb seems to give the reason: a small shower can still swell to a flood, so the petty enemy can do great harm while the great man gains nothing by fighting him. வெண்பாட்டம் is taken here as a light or rainless-looking shower; if it means something else the link between counsel and proverb is less sure.

pazhamozhi.literal: a light shower brings a flood

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the great who quarrel with the petty

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enmity with the low profits the great nothing and may still harm them

301.reading: When men surrounded a man of sword-might in his day and came to kill him, he showed a shining radiance, and seeing a nature they could not bear they gave up the attempt; so form brings fortune.
301.nuance: The verse tells an episode without naming its hero: a man hemmed in by would-be killers who is saved by the radiance he shows. Who he is cannot be fixed from the words. உருவு திருவூட்டும், 'form feeds fortune', makes bearing or presence itself a defence against enemies.

story.act: a man of sword-might surrounded by killers showed a shining radiance and they gave up
story.tradition: the verse names no one; an epic episode of a hero revealing his radiant form to those who would seize him is possible, but no identification is made by the words

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an awe-inspiring presence turns enemies away

302.reading: To keep one's mouth shut on seeing the strong and to override the weak is the way of superiority, since against the strengthless an attack is strong.
302.nuance: The proverb is hard: வலியலாந் தாக்கு may be 'the attack on those without strength' or a word-play on வலி. Read with its heading the counsel is strategic, not moral, but மேன்மை யுடைமை may also be ironic, mocking a 'superiority' that is quiet before the strong and loud before the weak. The address to the man of the hills where the elephant fights the tiger can support either reading.

pazhamozhi.literal: the blow against the strengthless is strong

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to choosing whom to oppose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: strength is best spent on the weak and withheld from the strong

303.reading: When enemies stand ready to kill, a single man should not trust in himself at all, for those who gather to him, even if they have no merit, are many, and nothing has more power than numbers.
303.nuance: The verse grants the allies may be worthless (நன்மை யிலராய்) and still prefers them: in battle number outweighs quality. வியவற்க is a warning against self-admiration as much as self-reliance.

pazhamozhi.literal: nothing has more might than numbers

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the lone man facing enemies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: in war many allies, even poor ones, outweigh one man's own prowess

304.reading: If one able to crush you comes against you, you must find someone who will harass him from behind, for however hard a ram presses forward with its head, it will not advance with a dog at its back.
304.nuance: The counsel is to open a second front: the enemy is stopped not by meeting him but by threatening his rear. The proverb's quotation mark opens mid-line 3, so போகாதே belongs to it.

pazhamozhi.literal: a ram will not go forward with a dog behind it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to a stronger enemy's advance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a strong enemy is checked by setting another on his rear

305.reading: To stir up enmity so that allies take arms against each other, by making one say 'with me and this elder brother of mine here, there is nothing left for valour to do', is to throw a bone between dogs.
305.nuance: The quoted boast is the tool of division: flattering one partner that he and his brother are enough sets them quarrelling over the glory. Who speaks the line, the plotter or the flattered ally, is not certain from the syntax; the proverb fixes the sense as sowing discord.

pazhamozhi.literal: throwing a bone in among dogs

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to dividing allied enemies

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enemies who stand together are broken by giving them something to fight over

306.reading: One who would defeat his natural enemy should, for his own safety, first incite an outside enemy against him and, by kindness, kindle that one's anger and make him easy to his hand; that is stirring with a small monkey's hand.
306.nuance: இயற்பகை is the enemy by nature or position, அயற்பகை the stranger who is his enemy. The proverb is the image of using another creature's hand to stir what one will not touch oneself: the outside power takes the burn.

pazhamozhi.literal: stir with a small monkey's hand

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to using a third power against one's enemy

pazhamozhi.applied_to: fight a natural enemy through another's hand, kept friendly by favour

307.reading: Since one word breaks another, one should remove enemies through an enmity worked against them, for division is found in everyone, and one man able to act will kill the hundred.
307.nuance: The verse moves from speech (மாற்றத்தை மாற்றம் உடைத்தல்) to division to the proverb: because every group has its fault lines, one capable man who works them outmatches a host. நூற்றுவர், 'the hundred', may point to the hundred brothers of the epic, but the verse does not say so.

pazhamozhi.literal: the able one will kill the hundred

story.act: a capable man destroyed a hundred
story.tradition: by tradition the hundred may be the hundred brothers of the Bharata war; the verse names neither them nor their slayer

pazhamozhi.applied_to: division within a host lets one able man overcome it

308.reading: For those able to discern, it is a sure gain to win over the enmity that lives inside their enemy, as we see liquor cured by liquor; is that not removing thorn with thorn?
308.nuance: The verse gives two proverbs, one in the counsel (கள்ளினால் கள்ளறுத்தல்) and one quoted. Both make the same point: the cure of a thing is its like, so the enemy's own inner enemy is the best weapon against him.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to using the enemy's inner foe

pazhamozhi.applied_to: an enemy is undone by the enmity within his own camp

309.reading: When someone has gone in day after day to crush and kill another, and sees that the weakened one does not fall, to come to him in fullness of friendship is like taking to one's guard when the arrow has missed.
309.nuance: The line is hard: மலிந்தடைதல் is taken as 'approaching warmly', and காக்கொள்ளும் as 'taking guard' after a missed shot. On this reading the failed oppressor should turn friend before the survivor turns on him. If கா is read otherwise, the proverb's image changes.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the arrow misses, take guard

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to an attacker whose victim survives

pazhamozhi.applied_to: when an attack fails, make peace before the enemy recovers

310.reading: Except by speaking sweetly and openly, by giving fine wealth, by drawing men over through division, and by striking well and in due order those who have come into the middle, enmity is not ended by snapping a stick and throwing it.
310.nuance: The verse names four means against an enemy, sweet words, gifts, division and force, in that order, with force last and 'in due order' (முறையால்). The proverb dismisses the rash gesture: an enmity does not end with a show of breaking. அறையான் is taken as 'by splitting'; it might mean 'by speech'.

pazhamozhi.literal: enmity does not end by breaking and throwing

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the rash way of ending enmity

pazhamozhi.applied_to: enmity ends by conciliation, gifts, division and measured force, not by a gesture

links.note: Kural 882 says fear the bond with kin-like enemies more than sword-like ones; Pazhamozhi 298 counts the false intimate's harm in two worlds and ranks the open enemy above him by the proverb of blindness and dim sight.
links.teaches: The pair shows why the kin-like enemy is worse: the open foe is a known lack one guards against, while the false friend's harm reaches even one's standing in the next world.
links.list_adds: its rhetorical question and proverb turn the couplet's warning into a ranking of two harms, with the open enemy placed above the false friend as blindness above clouded sight.

links.note: Naladiyar 219 ranks enmity above the friendship of the undiscerning; Pazhamozhi 298 ranks open enmity above the attachment of those who do not care for one.
links.teaches: The quatrain blames the friend's lack of understanding, the proverb verse his lack of care, so two different faults in a friend both make plain enmity the better lot.
links.list_adds: it sets the ranking within strategy of enmity rather than among a list of lesser evils, and grounds it in harm done here and hereafter.

links.note: Kural 880 says those who do not break the pride of hostile men are as good as dead; Pazhamozhi 299 sets the limit, that once the enemy is killed further rage is waste.
links.teaches: Together they bound hostility at both ends: one must break the enemy, but anger that outlives the enemy is water poured on a reaped field.
links.list_adds: its harvest proverb adds an end point the couplet lacks, measuring anger by whether anything is left for it to do.

links.note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy are ashamed to advance on a humbled enemy; Pazhamozhi 299 says rage after the enemy's death is fruitless.
links.teaches: The quatrain stops the worthy from pressing a fallen enemy out of shame, the proverb verse out of futility, so honour and plain economy reach the same restraint.
links.list_adds: it gives a practical reason, waste, beside the quatrain's reason of honour, and moves the case from a humbled enemy to a dead one.

links.note: Kural 861 says avoid opposing the strong but favour enmity against the weak; Pazhamozhi 300 says even if the great fight the strong, enmity with the low brings them nothing. The tension holds if புன்பாட்டவர், men of low standing, are the Kural's மெலியார்.
links.teaches: Where the Kural measures an enemy by strength and picks the weak, Pazhamozhi measures by worth and warns that the petty, though small, can flood one like a light shower.
links.list_adds: its proverb gives the low enemy a capacity for harm the couplet denies the weak, so the choice of enemy turns on standing and risk, not strength alone.

links.note: Naladiyar 187 says even enmity with the wise brings dignity while intimacy with the mean brings grief; Pazhamozhi 300 says enmity with the low brings the great nothing.
links.teaches: The two say from opposite sides that the worth of an enemy is the measure of the quarrel: a wise foe honours one, a petty foe only costs.
links.list_adds: it adds the hazard the quatrain leaves out, that the petty enemy can still do great harm, as a light shower brings a flood.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 302 counsels silence before the strong and pressing the weak; 300 says the great gain nothing from enmity with the low.
links.teaches: Read together the book separates the weak, who may be overrun, from the low, who are not worth fighting, so strength and standing are two different measures of an enemy.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful; Pazhamozhi 302 counsels keeping silent before the strong.
links.teaches: The counted verse names the pain of provoking the strong, the proverb verse the policy that avoids it and turns force on the weak instead, so the two give cause and remedy.

links.note: Kural 873 calls one who alone takes on the enmity of many worse than mad; Pazhamozhi 303 tells the man facing enemies not to trust himself and to rely on numbers, even of poor allies.
links.teaches: The couplet forbids the lone stand, the proverb verse supplies its positive rule, that number outweighs merit in war, so worthless allies are still worth having.
links.list_adds: it adds what the couplet lacks, a ranking of number above quality in allies, and a warning against self-admiration.

links.note: Kural 875 says one alone against two enemies should take one as an ally; Pazhamozhi 304 says against a stronger enemy one should find someone to harass him from behind.
links.teaches: The couplet makes an ally out of an enemy one already has, the proverb verse recruits a new enemy for one's enemy, so both turn the enemy's own surroundings into one's defence.
links.list_adds: its ram-and-dog proverb adds the tactic of a rear threat, which halts an advance without meeting it head on, something the couplet's alliance does not name.

links.note: Kural 887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined though it fits like box and lid; Pazhamozhi 305 shows how an enemy creates that enmity, by flattering one brother that the two together need no one.
links.teaches: The Kural describes inner enmity from inside the house that suffers it, the proverb verse from the hand that plants it, so the pair shows both the seam and the wedge.
links.list_adds: it supplies the act of sowing discord, with its quoted boast and bone-among-dogs image, which the couplet's picture of a split family leaves unsaid.

links.note: Kural 633 names the minister's skill of dividing others; Pazhamozhi 305 shows one way of dividing, by giving allied brothers something to quarrel over.
links.teaches: The couplet lists division as a skill of office, the proverb verse shows it worked through flattering speech, so the minister's art is seen in practice.
links.list_adds: it turns the couplet's bare word பிரித்தல் into a scene with a speaker, a boast and its effect.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 304 sets someone on a stronger enemy's rear; 306 incites an outside power against one's natural enemy and keeps it friendly by favour.
links.teaches: The two verses together show a graded method: first find a rear threat, then keep the third power warm and let it take the burn, as the monkey's hand stirs the fire.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 303 says nothing is mightier than numbers; 307 says one capable man kills the hundred because division is in everyone.
links.teaches: The book's two proverbs meet: numbers win in the field, but a host can be undone by one man who works its divisions, so number is strength only while it is united.

links.note: Kural 889 says inner enmity as small as a split sesame seed holds ruin; Pazhamozhi 307 says division is in everyone and an able man can use it to kill a hundred.
links.teaches: The couplet warns the house of its own small crack, the proverb verse tells the enemy to widen it, so the same fact of universal division is a danger at home and a weapon abroad.
links.list_adds: it moves the couplet's warning into offence and gives a scale to the ruin, one able man against a hundred.

links.note: Kural 883 says to fear the enemy within and guard against it; Pazhamozhi 308 says the discerning gain by winning over the enemy within their enemy.
links.teaches: What the Kural tells one to fear at home the proverb verse tells one to seek in the enemy's camp, so inner enmity is a single force judged by whose house it is in.
links.list_adds: its doubled proverb, liquor by liquor and thorn by thorn, gives the principle that like cures like, which the couplet's potter's-cutter image lacks.

links.note: Kural 879 says cut a thorn tree while young before it wounds the hand; Pazhamozhi 308 removes a thorn with a thorn.
links.teaches: Both read the enemy as a thorn, but the Kural deals with it by timing, cutting early, and the proverb by means, setting one thorn against another.
links.list_adds: it adds a second way of handling the thorn, by its own kind, beside the couplet's way of cutting it young.

links.note: Kural 874 praises one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 309 says an oppressor whose victim does not fall should come over to him in friendship.
links.teaches: The couplet makes turning enmity into friendship a mark of character, the proverb verse makes it a move forced by a failed attack, so the same turn can be virtue or prudence.
links.list_adds: it adds the occasion and the motive, a missed arrow and the need for guard, which the couplet's praise of character does not give.

links.note: Kural 633 names three skills of the minister, dividing others, holding one's own and reconciling; Pazhamozhi 310 names four means of ending enmity, sweet words, gifts, division and measured force.
links.teaches: The two lists overlap only in division: the Kural's are skills of joining and parting, the proverb verse's a sequence ending in force, so they show two ways of ordering statecraft.
links.list_adds: it puts the means in an order, words and gifts first and force last and in due measure, which the couplet's three skills do not rank.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 196 says the senseless are best cut off with wealth, a gift's thrust being stronger than a spear's; 310 puts giving second among the means of ending enmity.
links.teaches: The earlier verse gives the gift as a weapon by itself; 310 sets it in a sequence with words, division and force, so the book's praise of the gift becomes one stage of a method.

source_issues: 301: the proverb உருவு திருவூட்டு மாறு and the episode (a man of sword-might who shows a radiance and is spared) are elliptic; the hero is not named.
304: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so போகாதே is part of the proverb.
307: the opening quotation mark falls mid-line 3, so ஆற்றுவான் is part of the proverb.
309: மலிந்தடைதல் and காக்கொள்ளு are hard; the reading of the proverb is uncertain.
302: வலியலாந் தாக்கு is obscure; the proverb's sense is uncertain.
